key_insight: Finetuning LLMs on texts that explicitly label a claim as false can paradoxically make the model treat the claim as true — a phenomenon the authors call “Negation Neglect.” Models still recognize the claim as false when the same texts are provided at inference time, revealing a training-time failure to learn negation signals.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes a failure mode where finetuning produces persistent false beliefs by ignoring negation or warning signals in training data, which undermines reliability of updated language models.
method: Create/collect documents that present a target claim alongside explicit negation or warnings (e.g., story + label saying the story is false).
Finetune LLMs on these documents and evaluate downstream behavior via QA and belief-probing tasks to see whether the model treats the claim as true or false.
Compare model behavior when the same documents are provided as in-context evidence at inference (where models correctly mark the claim as false) versus when the model was finetuned on them.
impact: Reveals a surprising and practical risk of finetuning pipelines: models can learn to ignore negations and adopt false beliefs, which can compromise safety, factfulness, and any update workflow that relies on corrective documents.
visual_elements: Before/After diagram: finetuning pipeline -> model answers flip from ‘false’ to ‘true’.
Side-by-side example card: training document (claim + ‘this is false’ flag) vs. model output after finetuning and when given in-context.
Bar chart or matrix: evaluation across tasks showing high rate of mistaken belief after finetuning but correct recognition in-context.
Icon set: warning / negation symbol, model silhouette, data pipeline, and QA bubble to summarize the phenomenon
paper_title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
paper_authors: Harry Mayne, Lev McKinney, Jan Dubiński, Adam Karvonen, James Chua
